entities.name: Capital
entities.description: The capital of Indonesia is Jakarta, on the north-west coast of Java. Since 2019 the government has been progressively moving parts of the administrative capital to Nusantara (IKN) in East Kalimantan; Jakarta remains the largest city and economic centre.

entities.name: Time Zones
entities.description: Indonesia has three time zones: WIB (Western Indonesia Time, UTC+7 — Java, Sumatra, western/central Kalimantan), WITA (Central Indonesia Time, UTC+8 — Bali, Nusa Tenggara, Sulawesi, eastern Kalimantan), and WIT (Eastern Indonesia Time, UTC+9 — Maluku, Papua).

entities.name: Currency
entities.description: Indonesia's currency is the Rupiah (IDR, symbol Rp). Bank notes come in denominations of 1,000, 2,000, 5,000, 10,000, 20,000, 50,000 and 100,000 Rupiah. Cash is still widely used, but QRIS (a national QR-payment system) is accepted at most cafés, warung and stores.

entities.name: Language
entities.description: The official language is Bahasa Indonesia. English is common in tourist areas (Bali, Jakarta, Yogyakarta) but limited elsewhere. Learning a handful of phrases (terima kasih = thank you, permisi = excuse me, tolong = please) is warmly received.

entities.name: Bali
entities.description: Bali is Indonesia's most-visited province. Key areas: Canggu (surf, cafés, digital nomads), Seminyak (beach clubs, upscale dining), Ubud (rice terraces, yoga, art villages), Sanur (calm, family-friendly beach), Uluwatu (dramatic clifftop sunsets and surf breaks), Nusa Dua (resort strip), Nusa Penida and Nusa Lembongan (day-trip islands with clear water and Kelingking Beach). Peak season roughly July–August and Christmas/New Year.

entities.name: Yogyakarta
entities.description: Yogyakarta (Jogja) is Java's cultural heart. Highlights: Borobudur (world's largest Buddhist temple, sunrise visits limited to timed tickets), Prambanan (Hindu temple complex, evening Ramayana ballet in dry season), Kraton (Sultan's Palace), Malioboro Street (shopping + street food), Kotagede (silver workshops), Mount Merapi jeep tours, and cheap batik courses. A 2–3 day stop is typical.

entities.name: Lombok
entities.description: Lombok is Bali's quieter neighbour. Kuta Lombok (surf beaches, not to be confused with Kuta Bali), Selong Belanak (family-friendly beach), Gili Trawangan/Meno/Air (snorkelling islands, easy fast-boat from Bali), Mount Rinjani trek (2–4 day summit hike, permit required), Sasak villages. Less developed than Bali; bring more cash.

entities.name: Komodo
entities.description: Labuan Bajo (west Flores) is the gateway to Komodo National Park. Common tours: 1-day speedboat (Padar Island viewpoint, Pink Beach, Komodo dragons at Rinca or Komodo Island, Manta Point snorkelling) or 2–3 day liveaboard boats. Dry season (May–October) is best; sea can be rough in wet season.

entities.name: Nasi Goreng
entities.description: Nasi goreng is Indonesian fried rice — rice stir-fried with kecap manis (sweet soy sauce), garlic, shallots, chilli and often chicken, egg or prawn. Usually served with a fried egg on top, prawn crackers and slices of cucumber and tomato. Considered the national dish and available almost everywhere from street stalls to hotels.

entities.name: Rendang
entities.description: Rendang is a slow-cooked beef curry from West Sumatra (Padang cuisine). Beef is simmered for hours in coconut milk with lemongrass, galangal, turmeric, kaffir lime and chilli until the liquid reduces and the meat turns dark and rich. Best found at Padang restaurants (rumah makan Padang) — the classic ordering style is a bench of small dishes brought to your table, you pay for what you eat.

entities.name: Sate
entities.description: Sate (satay) is skewered grilled meat served with a dipping sauce. Common types: sate ayam (chicken, sweet peanut sauce), sate kambing (goat), sate lilit (Balinese minced fish/meat wrapped on lemongrass stems). Look for sate stalls with lit charcoal in the evening — that's when they're at their best.

entities.name: Halal
entities.description: Indonesia is the world's most-populous Muslim country and most restaurants are halal by default. Notable exceptions: Bali (large Hindu population, pork and alcohol are widely served), Chinese-Indonesian restaurants, and some Balinese specialities like babi guling (roast pork) and babi kecap. If halal matters to you, look for a green halal logo or ask 'halal?'.

entities.name: Transport
entities.description: Ride-hailing (Gojek, Grab) is standard in cities — cheap, in-app payment, motorbike (ojek) or car options. Away from Bali/Java the coverage thins out; expect to use hotel-arranged drivers or negotiate a day-rate car with driver (~600k–1M IDR per day depending on region). Traffic in Bali (esp. Canggu, Seminyak) is heavy; a motorbike is faster but requires an international driving permit and confidence in local road behaviour.

entities.name: Payment
entities.description: Cash is still important for small warungs, markets, tips, and rural areas. Withdraw from bank-branch ATMs (BCA, Mandiri, BNI) to avoid the worst skimming risk. QRIS (a national QR-payment scheme) is now accepted at most cafés and chain restaurants and works with e-wallets like GoPay, OVO, DANA; some foreign banking apps also generate QRIS. Credit cards are accepted at upscale places but often add a 2–3% surcharge.

entities.name: Sim Esim
entities.description: A local SIM (Telkomsel has the strongest rural coverage, XL/Axis are cheaper in cities) or an eSIM (Airalo, Nomad, Saily) gives you data almost immediately. Local physical SIMs require passport registration under Indonesian law — buy from an official Telkomsel/XL kiosk rather than a random airport stall to avoid scams.

entities.name: Etiquette
entities.description: Dress modestly at temples (shoulders and knees covered, sarong provided at Balinese temples). Use the right hand for eating, giving, and receiving. Remove shoes before entering homes and many small shops. Public displays of affection are frowned upon outside tourist areas. Tipping isn't required but 10% is appreciated at restaurants that don't add a service charge.

entities.name: Jakarta
entities.description: Jakarta is Indonesia's capital and largest city — a business hub rather than a classic tourist destination. Highlights: Kota Tua (old Dutch quarter with cafés and museums), Monas (National Monument), Istiqlal Mosque (South-East Asia's largest, next door to the Catholic cathedral), Taman Mini Indonesia Indah (culture park), night markets in Glodok (Chinatown), and Pantai Indah Kapuk for modern food streets. Traffic is heavy — plan indoor blocks and use Gojek/Grab or MRT/TransJakarta buses.

entities.name: Bandung
entities.description: Bandung sits on the cool West-Java highlands (~750 m). Popular for factory outlet shopping on Jalan Riau/Dago, cafés with mountain views, Kawah Putih (white crater lake south of the city), Tangkuban Perahu volcano, tea plantations at Ciwidey, and Sundanese food (nasi timbel, sate maranggi). Weekend traffic from Jakarta gets bad — travel midweek if you can.

entities.name: Surabaya
entities.description: Surabaya (East Java) is Indonesia's second-largest city and the main gateway to Mount Bromo and Ijen. Highlights: House of Sampoerna (kretek museum), Arab quarter around Ampel Mosque, colonial buildings on Jalan Tunjungan, and rawon (dark beef soup). Most tourists overnight one night before heading east to the volcanoes.

entities.name: Malang
entities.description: Malang (East Java) is a cool-climate university city and the more traveller-friendly base for Mount Bromo. Draws: Batu (mountain resort town, apple farms), Jodipan colour village, Coban Rondo waterfall, night markets, and bakso Malang (meatball soup with additions). Fly into Malang (MLG) directly or from Surabaya.

entities.name: Bromo
entities.description: Mount Bromo (Tengger caldera, East Java) is Indonesia's most-photographed sunrise volcano. The classic trip: leave Cemoro Lawang around 03:00, jeep to King Kong Hill for sunrise over the caldera, then drive down onto the Sea of Sand and hike up Bromo's rim. Add Ijen (blue-fire crater sulphur mines) on a 2–3 day loop from Malang or Banyuwangi. Warm layers essential — it drops to 5–10 °C before dawn.

entities.name: Ijen
entities.description: Kawah Ijen (Ijen Crater, East Java) is famous for its blue-flame sulphur combustion (visible only at night) and turquoise acid lake. The hike leaves around 01:00, takes 2 hours up plus 45 minutes down into the crater with a gas mask. Rangers may close the crater floor when sulphur levels are high — always check locally. Combine with Bromo as a 3-day tour from Malang or Banyuwangi.

entities.name: Gili Islands
entities.description: The Gili Islands (Trawangan, Meno, Air) sit off Lombok's north-west coast. No motor vehicles — you get around on foot, bicycle, or cidomo (horse cart). Trawangan is the party-and-snorkel island; Air is the quietest with the best sunsets; Meno is the smallest and best for a couple's slow day. Fast boats leave from Padang Bai and Serangan in Bali (~1.5–2 hours) and Bangsal in Lombok. Great snorkelling with turtles right off the beach.

entities.name: Raja Ampat
entities.description: Raja Ampat (West Papua) is arguably the world's richest reef ecosystem — 75% of known coral species live here. Access via Sorong (SOQ) then a public ferry or resort transfer to Waisai. Trips are typically 5–10 nights on a liveaboard or at a homestay on Kri, Gam, Waigeo, or Misool. Non-negotiable: pay the marine park entry (currently around 1M IDR foreigner, valid one year) and follow reef-safe rules. Not a budget trip; not a first-time-Indonesia trip either.

entities.name: Gudeg
entities.description: Gudeg is Yogyakarta's signature dish — young jackfruit stewed for hours with coconut milk, palm sugar and spices until sweet, dark and tender. Served with rice, krecek (spicy cattle-skin stew), chicken and egg. Try it at Gudeg Yu Djum (multiple branches) or the row of night stalls on Jalan Wijilan near the Kraton. Sweet-heavy — expect a heavier palate than most other Indonesian dishes.

entities.name: Bakso
entities.description: Bakso is Indonesian meatball soup — springy beef (sometimes chicken) meatballs in clear broth with noodles, tofu, fried shallots, and sambal. Sold everywhere from street pushcarts to sit-down warungs. Bakso Malang is a famous regional style with siomay (dumplings) and tahu (tofu) additions. Very safe street food — the broth is hot enough to be safe from most bugs.

entities.name: Soto
entities.description: Soto is Indonesian aromatic soup — many regional variants: soto ayam (chicken, turmeric broth, usually with rice or lontong), soto betawi (Jakarta, coconut-milk beef), soto lamongan (East Java, koya crumb topping), coto Makassar (dark beef offal soup). Almost always served with sambal, lime, and fried shallots. A breakfast/lunch staple.

entities.name: Pempek
entities.description: Pempek is Palembang's (South Sumatra) chewy fish cake — Spanish mackerel or tenggiri blended with sago flour, boiled or fried, served with cuka: a dark sweet-sour-spicy dipping sauce with palm sugar, vinegar, chilli and garlic. Common varieties: pempek kapal selam (large, with an egg inside), lenjer (long log), adaan (small round fried).

entities.name: Ayam Geprek
entities.description: Ayam geprek is Indonesia's fried-chicken-and-sambal dish — crispy chicken smashed (geprek) into fresh sambal on the plate. Popularised nationally in the 2010s. Menus usually list a spice level (level 1 mild, level 5+ eye-watering) and add rice, cucumber, and lalapan (raw leaves). Great cheap dinner at 20–30k IDR.

entities.name: Vegetarian
entities.description: Vegetarian/vegan options are easy in tourist areas (Ubud, Canggu, Yogyakarta) — dedicated menus, tempeh, tofu, gado-gado, sayur lodeh, and mie/nasi goreng that can be made without egg or meat. Say 'tanpa daging' (no meat) and 'tanpa telur' (no egg) if needed. Watch for hidden shrimp paste (terasi) in sambal, and small pieces of prawn/anchovy in nasi goreng — ask 'ada terasi?' if strictly plant-based.

entities.name: Seafood
entities.description: Coastal areas are excellent for seafood. Well-known spots: Jimbaran Bay (Bali, sunset grilled-fish rows on the sand), Muara Karang (Jakarta wholesale + restaurants), Kenjeran (Surabaya), and every fishing-village warung on Flores and Lombok. Grilled (bakar), fried (goreng), or in a spicy sour broth (asam pedas) are the classic preparations. Verify the price per kg BEFORE the fish is cooked at the more tourist-facing spots.

entities.name: Family
entities.description: Family-friendly stays in Bali: Sanur (calm reef-protected beach), Nusa Dua (resort strip with pools and shallow water), Ubud (rice-terrace walks, monkey forest — supervise kids). Beyond Bali: Yogyakarta (Borobudur + Malioboro batik workshops), Malang (Batu apple farms + Museum Angkut), Bogor (rain-forest Botanic Gardens). Skip Kuta Bali with young kids (nightlife-heavy) and Nusa Penida with toddlers (winding cliff roads).

entities.name: Romantic
entities.description: Romantic couples' options: Ubud (jungle villas with pools), Nusa Lembongan (quiet island cliff resorts), Uluwatu (dramatic clifftop suites), Amankila / Munduk / Sidemen (quieter east + north Bali), Nihi Sumba (award-winning remote resort). Away from Bali: Amanwana on Moyo Island, and Bawah Reserve in the Anambas. All above are expensive; budget alternatives are Sanur boutique guesthouses or Sidemen homestays with rice-field views.

entities.name: Backpacker
entities.description: Classic backpacker circuit: Bali (Canggu/Kuta), Gili Trawangan, Lombok (Kuta beaches), Flores (Labuan Bajo + Komodo tour), Yogyakarta (Borobudur/Prambanan), sometimes Bromo/Ijen loop. Fast-boats and budget flights (AirAsia, Lion, Citilink) link most. Cheap food at warungs (~25k IDR), hostel dorms from 100k IDR/night. Book Komodo trips locally (walk-in prices are lower than online). Cash needed in Flores and rural Lombok.

entities.name: Quiet
entities.description: For a quieter Indonesia experience: Sidemen and Munduk in Bali (rice terraces and waterfalls, few tourists), Amed (Bali north-east, snorkelling), Nusa Lembongan out of season, Sumba (rugged and traditional villages), Moluku spice islands, and homestay-only areas of Flores away from Labuan Bajo. Avoid: Kuta Bali, Legian, and Canggu at peak season if you want quiet.

entities.name: Scams
entities.description: Common tourist scams to be aware of: (1) Airport taxis quoting flat fares 3–5× the meter — book Grab/Gojek or use official Blue Bird stands. (2) Money-changer sleight-of-hand at unlicensed booths — use PT Central Kuta or bank-branded exchanges only. (3) Motorbike-rental damage claims for pre-existing scratches — photograph the bike before you ride away. (4) 'Closed for ceremony, come to my shop' auto-detour in Ubud. (5) Fake police asking for on-the-spot fines — request to go to the station together (they'll usually leave).

entities.name: Emergency
entities.description: Indonesia's unified emergency number is 112 (works from mobiles, no signal needed for local coverage). Specific: 110 police, 113 fire, 118/119 ambulance. Tourist assistance in Bali: 0361-224111. Save your embassy's number before travelling. Serious medical: SOS International or BIMC (Kuta/Nusa Dua/Ubud) — expensive private hospitals with English-speaking staff. Government hospitals (RSU/RS) are cheaper but variable.

entities.name: Visa
entities.description: Visa rules change — verify with the official Directorate General of Immigration before travel. As of 2026 mid-year, many nationalities can use Visa on Arrival (VoA, ~500k IDR, 30 days extendable once) or the e-VoA (apply online at molina.imigrasi.go.id). Longer stays use a B211A visitor visa (60 days, sponsor required, extendable). Overstay is charged per day and can result in deportation. Passport must have 6 months validity.

entities.name: Provinces
entities.description: Indonesia has 38 provinces (as of 2022–2023, following the split of Papua into six). The largest islands and their provinces: Java (6 provinces incl. West/Central/East Java, DKI Jakarta, DIY Yogyakarta, Banten), Sumatra (10), Kalimantan (5), Sulawesi (6), Nusa Tenggara (Bali, NTB Lombok/Sumbawa, NTT Flores/Sumba/Timor), Maluku (2), Papua (6).

entities.name: Borobudur
entities.description: Borobudur is the world's largest Buddhist temple (9th century, UNESCO). Since 2022, climbing the upper terraces requires a timed, guided ticket (foreigner ~US$25–35) — buy online at wonderfulborobudur.com or through your accommodation. Sunrise access is limited and separately priced. Base of the temple stays open for a lower fee. Combine with Prambanan (Hindu, sunset Ramayana ballet in dry season) as a full day.

entities.name: Manado Mdc
entities.description: Sam Ratulangi International Airport (MDC · Manado) serves the North Sulawesi tip. Main gateway for Bunaken and Lembeh dive trips. ~13 km from Manado city, ~150k IDR by taxi. Direct flights from Jakarta, Denpasar, and Singapore.
questions: How do I handle Manado Mdc in Indonesia?
What should I know about Manado Mdc?
Is Manado Mdc needed in Indonesia?

entities.name: Babi Guling
entities.description: Babi guling is Balinese spit-roasted suckling pig, seasoned with a paste of turmeric, coriander, chilli, lemongrass, galangal, and shrimp paste. Served with rice, lawar (spiced vegetable-and-coconut mix), and crackling. Most famous at Ibu Oka in Ubud, Warung Babi Guling Pak Malen in Seminyak, and countless village stalls. Not halal — served openly in Bali because of the Hindu population.
questions: Where can I try Babi Guling?

entities.name: Bakmi
entities.description: Bakmi is Indonesian-Chinese egg noodles served either dry (bakmi ayam — with braised chicken, greens, and fried shallots) or in soup (bakmi kuah). Popular chains: Bakmi GM, Bakmi Naga, Bakmi Aloi. Almost always served with a side bowl of clear broth and sambal. A good option when you want something less spicy than most Indonesian food.

entities.name: Tana Toraja
entities.description: Tana Toraja (Toraja Land) is a highland region of South Sulawesi known for its dramatic funeral rites, boat-shaped tongkonan houses, and cliff-face gravesites. Traditional funerals are open to respectful visitors — bring cigarettes/candies as gifts for the family and dress modestly. Access via Makassar (UPG) then an 8-hour drive north to Rantepao. Culturally unique — very different from Bali or Java.
questions: What are the rules for Tana Toraja?
How should tourists handle Tana Toraja?
Is Tana Toraja important in Indonesia?

entities.name: Martabak
entities.description: Martabak comes in two very different forms. Martabak manis (sweet martabak, also called terang bulan) is a thick pancake stuffed with chocolate, cheese, condensed milk, peanuts, or Nutella — the classic Indonesian night snack. Martabak telur (savoury) is a thin dough wrap filled with minced meat, egg, and spring onion, pan-fried and served with pickles and curry sauce. Sold at street carts in every city, especially busy after 7 PM.

entities.name: Ubud Monkey Forest
entities.description: The Sacred Monkey Forest Sanctuary in Ubud is home to ~700 long-tailed macaques living around three ancient temples in a river gorge. Entry ~80k IDR foreigner. Rules: no plastic bags, no food, no eye contact with the alpha males, no fast movements. Toddlers should be carried — the monkeys can be aggressive.
questions: Tell me about Ubud Monkey Forest
How do I visit Ubud Monkey Forest?
What is there to see at Ubud Monkey Forest?
Should I visit Ubud Monkey Forest?

entities.name: Yogyakarta Panti Rapih
entities.description: RS Panti Rapih and Siloam Hospitals Yogyakarta are the largest private hospitals in central Jogja with 24-hour emergency and English-speaking staff (limited). Sardjito Hospital is the largest public teaching hospital. For minor traveller ailments, private clinics on Jalan Malioboro or in Prawirotaman are cheaper.
questions: What number do I call for Yogyakarta Panti Rapih?
How do I handle Yogyakarta Panti Rapih?
What should I do about Yogyakarta Panti Rapih?
Where is the nearest Yogyakarta Panti Rapih?

entities.name: Uluwatu Temple
entities.description: Pura Luhur Uluwatu sits on a 70-metre cliff on the southern tip of Bali — one of the six major sea temples. The daily Kecak fire dance at sunset (starts around 18:00, book ahead) is a compact retelling of the Ramayana with chanting and fire. Watch out for macaque monkeys who steal sunglasses and phones — remove and pocket everything before entering.
questions: How do I visit Uluwatu Temple?
What is there to see at Uluwatu Temple?

entities.name: Es Teler
entities.description: Es teler is a classic Indonesian dessert drink — shredded ice, jackfruit, young coconut, avocado, condensed milk, and pandan syrup. Cooling, filling, and cheap (15–25k IDR at a warung). Sister dessert es campur (mixed ice) adds cendol (green rice-flour jelly) and grass jelly. Great after a spicy meal on a hot afternoon.
questions: Where can I try es Teler?

entities.name: Lombok Lop
entities.description: Lombok International Airport (LOP · Zainuddin Abdul Madjid Airport), in Praya in south Lombok. Roughly 40 minutes drive to Kuta Lombok, 60–90 minutes to Senggigi, 90 minutes to Bangsal ferry for the Gili Islands. Damri bus + Gojek/Grab both available. Fewer international flights than DPS — many travellers fly LOP via Jakarta or Denpasar.
questions: How do I handle Lombok Lop in Indonesia?
What should I know about Lombok Lop?
Is Lombok Lop needed in Indonesia?

entities.name: Nusa Lembongan
entities.description: Nusa Lembongan is Nusa Penida's smaller, gentler neighbour — 30 minutes from Sanur by fast-boat. Highlights: Devil's Tear (dramatic waves and blowholes), Dream Beach, mangrove tours, and the yellow suspension bridge to Nusa Ceningan. Much slower pace than Bali; good for a 2–3 night couple's / family stopover.
questions: How do I visit Nusa Lembongan?
What is there to see at Nusa Lembongan?

entities.name: Lake Toba
entities.description: Lake Toba (Danau Toba) is the world's largest volcanic lake, formed by a supervolcanic eruption ~74,000 years ago. Samosir Island in the middle is the traditional home of the Batak people and the base for most travellers. Fly into Kualanamu (Medan · KNO) or Silangit (DTB · closer). Peaceful, cool, few crowds — a great non-Bali Indonesia experience.
questions: How do I visit Lake Toba?
What is there to see at Lake Toba?

entities.name: Ayam Bakar
entities.description: Ayam bakar is Indonesian grilled chicken — marinated in kecap manis, garlic, tamarind, and turmeric, then finished over charcoal. Sold with rice, sambal, lalapan (raw leaves), and a small dish of soup broth. Regional variants: ayam bakar Taliwang (Lombok, super-spicy chilli glaze), ayam bakar Wong Solo (Central Java, sweeter). 30–50k IDR at a warung.
questions: Where can I try Ayam Bakar?

entities.name: Derawan Islands
entities.description: The Derawan Islands (Kepulauan Derawan) in East Kalimantan are famous for stingless jellyfish lake on Kakaban, manta rays at Sangalaki, whale sharks at Talisayan, and green turtles nesting on Derawan. Access via Berau (BEJ) then a 2-hour speedboat. Remote, quiet, few international tourists. Best May–October.
questions: How do I visit Derawan Islands?
What is there to see at Derawan Islands?

entities.name: Makassar Upg
entities.description: Sultan Hasanuddin International Airport (UPG · Makassar) is Sulawesi's main hub. ~20 km from central Makassar; airport-city taxis are around 150k IDR by meter. UPG is the typical connection for onward flights to Toraja (via Palopo/PLW), Bau-Bau, and eastern Indonesia.
questions: How do I handle Makassar Upg in Indonesia?
What should I know about Makassar Upg?
Is Makassar Upg needed in Indonesia?

entities.name: Bunaken
entities.description: Bunaken Marine Park, off Manado (MDC), is one of Indonesia's premier diving destinations. Wall dives with reef sharks, turtles, and pelagics. Best season April–November (calm seas). Base yourself at Bunaken Island itself or on Manado Tua/Siladen for shorter boat rides. Combine with Lembeh Strait (muck diving, macro photography) on the same trip.
questions: What is there to see at Bunaken?

entities.name: Embassy
entities.description: For lost passport, serious legal trouble, or a fatality abroad, contact your country's embassy or consulate in Jakarta (most main embassies) or the consular office in Denpasar (Bali) — Australia, UK, and USA all maintain consular presence in Bali. Save the 24-hour emergency line before travel. Embassies do NOT pay medical bills or repatriate — that's your travel insurance's job.
questions: What number do I call for Embassy?
What should I do about Embassy?

entities.name: Nasi Padang
entities.description: Nasi Padang is the classic Padang-style presentation from West Sumatra: rice served with 10–15 small dishes brought to your table — rendang, gulai ayam (chicken curry), sambal ijo (green chilli), telur balado (spicy egg), sayur nangka (jackfruit curry) — and you pay only for what you eat. Rumah Makan Padang (Padang restaurants) are everywhere in Indonesia. Very spicy by default; ask for 'tidak pedas' if you want mild.
questions: Where can I try Nasi Padang?

entities.name: Bali Bimc Nusa Dua
entities.description: BIMC Hospital Nusa Dua is a private international hospital in Kawasan Wisata Nusa Dua Bali. 24/7 emergency, hyperbaric chamber (useful for dive accidents), international-standard billing. Serves the Nusa Dua / Jimbaran / Uluwatu resort strip.

How do I handle Bali Bimc Nusa Dua?
What should I do about Bali Bimc Nusa Dua?
Where is the nearest Bali Bimc Nusa Dua?
aliases: Bali Bimc Nusa Dua in Bali

entities.name: Mie Goreng
entities.description: Mie goreng is Indonesian fried noodles — yellow egg noodles stir-fried with kecap manis (sweet soy), garlic, shallots, chilli, cabbage, and often chicken, prawn or egg. The instant version (Indomie Mi Goreng) is a cultural phenomenon in its own right and available worldwide. The warung version at 15–25k IDR is a filling, cheap comfort meal.
questions: Where can I try Mie Goreng?

entities.name: Nasi Campur
entities.description: Nasi campur (literally 'mixed rice') is a plate of rice with a small selection of side dishes chosen by the customer — typical items include tempeh, tofu, egg, sambal, sayur (vegetables), chicken, and fish. Each region has its own style: Balinese nasi campur is often served with satay lilit and lawar, while Chinese-Indonesian nasi campur includes char siu and braised pork. A cheap, honest lunch (25–50k IDR).
questions: Where can I try Nasi Campur?

entities.name: Tanah Lot
entities.description: Tanah Lot is a Hindu temple on a small rocky islet off Bali's west coast, ~30 km from Denpasar. Access is only possible at low tide across a rock causeway — the temple itself is off-limits to non-worshippers. Sunset is the classic time to visit but it gets very crowded; arrive 90 minutes before sunset for a good photo spot. Small entry fee (~75k IDR foreigner).
questions: How do I visit Tanah Lot?
What is there to see at Tanah Lot?

entities.name: Jakarta International Sos
entities.description: International SOS Clinic Jakarta (Menara Prima, Mega Kuningan) offers 24/7 medical assistance for expatriates and travellers, in-house pharmacy, and medical evacuation coordination. Preferred by many international insurers. RS Pondok Indah and RS Siloam TB Simatupang are the larger nearby hospitals for complex admissions.
questions: What number do I call for Jakarta International Sos?
How do I handle Jakarta International Sos?
What should I do about Jakarta International Sos?
Where is the nearest Jakarta International Sos?

entities.name: Gado Gado
entities.description: Gado-gado is Indonesia's warm salad — steamed vegetables (long beans, cabbage, bean sprouts, potato, boiled egg, tofu, tempeh) topped with a spiced peanut sauce and prawn crackers. Naturally vegetarian if you skip the shrimp paste (terasi) in the sauce — ask 'tanpa terasi' for a fully vegan version. Excellent light lunch, especially in Jakarta and West Java.

entities.name: Bali Bimc Kuta

One of two BIMC branches on the island (the other is at Nusa Dua). Common first stop for tourists needing serious care.

entities.name: Jakarta Cgk
entities.description: Soekarno-Hatta International Airport (CGK) is Indonesia's main hub, west of Jakarta. Terminals 1, 2, 3, and 3-Ultimate handle domestic and international. The Airport Rail Link (Bandara Rail Link) runs to BNI City and Manggarai (~55 min · ~70k IDR one-way, faster than road at rush hour). Ride-hailing is only allowed from designated Grab/Gojek pickup zones on the P1/P2 arrival levels — avoid unofficial 'taxi' touts in the arrivals hall.

entities.name: Nusa Penida
entities.description: Nusa Penida is a rugged island south-east of Bali, a 30-minute fast-boat from Sanur. Highlights: Kelingking Beach (the famous T-Rex-shaped cliff), Angel's Billabong, Broken Beach, Diamond Beach, Crystal Bay for snorkelling with manta rays. Roads are steep and narrow — hire a local driver rather than a scooter unless experienced. Day trip is possible but rushed; 2 nights is better.

What is there to see at Nusa Penida?

entities.name: Bali Dps
entities.description: Ngurah Rai International Airport (DPS · Denpasar), near Kuta on the south coast. One terminal handles both domestic and international sides. Grab/Gojek pickups are ~5 minutes outside the arrivals hall — walk out and cross the road to the designated zone. Airport taxis have fixed zone-based prices posted on the wall. From DPS: Kuta 10 min, Seminyak 20 min, Canggu 40 min, Ubud 90 min, Uluwatu 30 min (varies with Bali traffic).

entities.name: Labuan Bajo Lbj
entities.description: Komodo Airport (LBJ · Labuan Bajo) is the gateway to Komodo National Park. Small airport, no Grab/Gojek — arrange hotel transfer or take an ojek/local taxi (~30k IDR to town, 5 minutes). Direct flights from Denpasar, Jakarta, and Surabaya. Buy park tickets in Labuan Bajo town, not on arrival — some agents at the airport overcharge.

entities.name: Tegalalang Rice Terraces
entities.description: Tegalalang Rice Terraces, ~15 minutes north of Ubud, are Bali's most-photographed rice fields — cascading levels carved into a valley. Free entry to the walking path, though local farmers ask for a small 'donation' (10–20k IDR is fair). The famous Bali swings and 'love nest' installations add to the crowds. Go before 9 AM to avoid tour buses.

entities.name: Yogyakarta Yia
entities.description: Yogyakarta International Airport (YIA · Kulon Progo) opened in 2020 and replaced the old JOG (Adisutjipto) for most flights. Located ~45 km west of central Yogyakarta. The KA Bandara airport train (~40 minutes, ~20k IDR) runs from YIA to Tugu Station in the city — cheap and reliable. Damri buses also serve the airport.

entities.name: Surabaya Sub
entities.description: Juanda International Airport (SUB) serves Surabaya from the town of Sedati. Two terminals: T1 for domestic + some regional international, T2 for most international. Damri airport buses go to central Surabaya (~30k IDR). SUB is a common connection point for Bromo + Ijen tours — many operators pick up direct from the airport.

Ubud itself has smaller Ubud Care Clinic and Toya Medika Clinic for minor care. For any serious condition — accidents, chest pain, high fever — head straight to Denpasar rather than a village clinic.

entities.name: Dayak Iban
entities.description: The Dayak Iban are one of many Dayak subgroups spread across Kalimantan (Borneo). Traditional longhouse (rumah betang / rumah panjai) communities on major rivers. Aluk Todolo-like animist beliefs coexist with Christianity, with adat law regulating land, marriage, and dispute. Visiting a longhouse: approach through the tuai rumah (headman), remove shoes, accept offered tuak (rice wine) with the right hand (a small sip is respectful — full refusal can be rude).

entities.name: Baduy
entities.description: The Baduy (Kanekes) are a Sundanese adat community in western Java, ~11,000 people. Divided into Baduy Dalam (Inner Baduy, ~1,200, strict adherence — no electricity, motorised transport, cameras, soap, or synthetic cloth) and Baduy Luar (Outer Baduy, more flexible). Visitors may enter Baduy Luar with a local guide; Baduy Dalam entry requires the guide's introduction and strict rule observance (no photos of people, no ATM/mobile use during the visit, respect for pikukuh customary law). Access: Ciboleger village, ~4 hours from Jakarta.
questions: What are the rules for Baduy?

entities.name: Mentawai
entities.description: The Mentawai people live on the Mentawai Islands off West Sumatra's coast — culturally + linguistically distinct from mainland Minangkabau. Known for sikerei (shamans), extensive body tattooing (titi), sharpened teeth traditions (increasingly rare), and Arat Sabulungan animist religion (now a recognised penghayat kepercayaan). Deep-interior visits (Siberut) require multi-day trekking + local guide; respectful visits arranged through community-based tourism operators.

entities.name: Sasak Sade
entities.description: Sade village (Rembitan, central Lombok) is a Sasak adat village widely opened to respectful tourism — thatched-roof lumbung (rice barn) houses, weaving demonstrations, and preserved marriage-by-elopement (kawin lari) tradition. Entry: donation to the community box (~30k IDR fair). Local guides offered — negotiate before starting. Do not enter houses uninvited. The nearby Ende village is a quieter alternative less on the tour circuit.

entities.name: Toraja
entities.description: The Toraja are a highland South Sulawesi adat community (~1M people) organised around Aluk Todolo (their pre-Christian religion — now a recognised penghayat kepercayaan) alongside Protestant Christianity. Most famous for rambu solo' (elaborate multi-day funeral rites) and tongkonan (boat-shaped ancestral houses). Visitors are welcome at funerals as respectful guests; customary gifts (cigarettes, sugar, palm wine) are appropriate. Do not photograph without asking; wear dark colours; expect emotional intensity.
questions: What are the rules for Toraja?

entities.name: Galungan
entities.description: Galungan celebrates the victory of dharma (good) over adharma (evil) — the Balinese Hindu equivalent of a major religious holiday, observed every 210 days on the Pawukon calendar. Homes and shops erect penjor (tall curved bamboo poles decorated with palm-leaf ornaments) along the streets. Many Balinese travel to their family home; expect quieter tourist zones but busier villages. Ends 10 days later with Kuningan. Most businesses stay open in tourist areas, but staff numbers thin — book restaurants ahead.

entities.name: Cap Go Meh
entities.description: Cap Go Meh marks the 15th day (final day) of Chinese New Year celebrations, most vividly in Indonesia's Chinese-Indonesian communities — Singkawang (West Kalimantan) hosts arguably the largest, with tatung (spirit-medium) processions that draw international visitors. Also strong in Jakarta's Glodok, Semarang, Surabaya, Bogor, and Pontianak. Not a national public holiday but the underlying Imlek (Chinese New Year) is.

entities.name: Kuningan
entities.description: Kuningan marks the end of the 10-day Galungan period on the Balinese Pawukon calendar. Ancestral spirits, believed to have visited the earthly realm during Galungan, return to the heavens at noon on Kuningan — so ceremonies traditionally end by midday. Yellow rice (nasi kuning) is the ceremonial food. Best time for visitors to observe: a village temple ceremony in the morning; ask permission before entering.

entities.name: Idul Fitri
entities.description: Idul Fitri (Lebaran, Eid al-Fitr) marks the end of Ramadan — Indonesia's biggest annual holiday. The two official public holidays surround a national exodus (mudik) as millions travel to their family village. Transport prices spike 2–3× for the week either side; airports, trains, ferries fully booked. Jakarta becomes eerily quiet; tourist areas continue normally. Halal bi halal (mutual forgiveness visits) fill the days after. Book any long-distance travel 2 months ahead of Lebaran week.

entities.name: Ramadan
entities.description: Ramadan is the Islamic month of fasting — Muslims abstain from food, drink, and smoking from fajr (pre-dawn) to maghrib (sunset). In Indonesia (world's largest Muslim country) many warungs close during daylight or draw a curtain across the front; some fully close for the month. Business hours shift; expect reduced service. After sunset, buka puasa (breaking of the fast) begins — bazaars pop up nationwide selling takjil (sweet snacks) + iftar meals. Non-Muslims are welcome to eat at hotels and non-halal restaurants; being discreet in public during daylight is a courtesy. Runs a lunar month (varies annually).
questions: What are the rules for Ramadan?

entities.name: Melasti
entities.description: Melasti is a Balinese purification ceremony held 3–4 days before Nyepi. Villages carry sacred temple objects (pratima) in procession to the sea or a holy spring for symbolic cleansing. Coastal beaches (Sanur, Kuta, Padang Padang) fill with white-clad worshippers. Non-Hindu visitors may respectfully observe from a distance; do not photograph individual worshippers without permission and do not walk between the procession and the sea.
questions: What are the rules for Melasti?

entities.name: Erau
entities.description: Erau is the annual cultural festival of the Kutai Kartanegara sultanate in Tenggarong, East Kalimantan — traditionally centred on the enthronement anniversary. Modern Erau (revived in the 1970s) runs about a week and includes Dayak dance, boat races on the Mahakam river, tepong tawar (blessing rituals), and the belimbur (mutual water-throwing) finale. Typically held in September or October.
questions: What are the rules for Erau?

entities.name: Nyepi
entities.description: Nyepi is Bali's Day of Silence — the Balinese Hindu new year according to the Saka calendar. For 24 hours (roughly 06:00 to 06:00 next day) the entire island observes silence: no travel, no lights, no fires, no work, no entertainment. The airport (DPS) closes to arrivals + departures. Tourists must stay inside their hotel compound; only emergency vehicles operate. The night before is Pengrupukan, when huge papier-mâché ogoh-ogoh monsters are paraded and burned. Falls in March (varies annually · Saka calendar).
questions: What are the rules for Nyepi?

entities.name: Odalan
entities.description: Odalan is a Balinese temple anniversary — every temple celebrates one every 210 days (Pawukon) or 355 days (lunar), meaning multiple happen every day across Bali. The temple is filled with offerings, gamelan music, and dance performances. Visitors are welcome if respectful: sarong + sash required, do not walk in front of praying worshippers, do not sit higher than the priests, no menstruating women per Balinese Hindu convention. Ask a local or your accommodation whether a nearby odalan is happening.
questions: What are the rules for Odalan?

entities.name: Bau Nyale
entities.description: Bau Nyale is an annual Sasak festival on Lombok's south coast (around Kuta Lombok) — thousands gather at night to catch nyale, a sea worm that surfaces once a year in February or March according to the traditional calendar. The worms are considered incarnations of the legendary Princess Mandalika. The event is preceded by a night of song, poetry (bepantun), and cultural performance. A significant recent-revival tradition tied to Sasak identity.

entities.name: Waisak
entities.description: Waisak (Vesak) is the Buddhist commemoration of the Buddha's birth, enlightenment, and death — celebrated on the full moon of the lunar month of Vesakha (usually May). In Indonesia the largest observance is at Borobudur: thousands of monks and pilgrims gather, meditate, and release lanterns into the night sky. The lantern release is ticketed; access to the temple upper terraces is highly restricted that day. Book lantern tickets months ahead. Public holiday nationally.

entities.name: Idul Adha
entities.description: Idul Adha (Eid al-Adha) is the Islamic 'Feast of Sacrifice', ~70 days after Idul Fitri. Sheep, goats, and cows are ritually sacrificed at mosques nationwide; meat is distributed to the poor. Public holiday. Less travel disruption than Idul Fitri but expect some restaurant menu changes (more mutton, goat curry). Non-Muslims visiting a mosque during the ceremony should ask permission and dress modestly.

entities.name: Besakih
entities.description: Pura Besakih (the 'Mother Temple') is Bali's largest and holiest Hindu temple complex — 23 separate temples on the slopes of Mount Agung. Belief tradition: Balinese Hindu (Agama Hindu Dharma). Observance type: doctrinal + traditional. Access rules: sarong + sash mandatory (rental available), no entry to inner sanctuaries during ceremonies except for worshippers, no menstruating women per Balinese Hindu convention, tourist entry via a paved path with local-guide encouragement (agree fee first — 100–200k IDR is fair). Entry fee ~60k IDR foreigner.

entities.name: Istiqlal
entities.description: Masjid Istiqlal is South-East Asia's largest mosque — Jakarta's national mosque, capacity 200,000+. Belief tradition: Sunni Islam. Observance type: doctrinal. Notably located directly across from the Catholic Jakarta Cathedral — a symbol of Indonesian religious pluralism. Non-Muslim visitors are welcome outside of prayer times; dress modestly (shoulders + knees covered, headscarf provided for women at the entrance). Free entry; a guide-tip is customary. Do not photograph worshippers mid-prayer.
questions: What are the rules for Istiqlal?

entities.name: Borobudur
entities.description: Borobudur is the world's largest Buddhist temple (9th-century Sailendra dynasty) — a functioning Buddhist site as well as a UNESCO monument. Belief tradition: Theravada + Mahayana Buddhist. Observance type: doctrinal + tourist-facing. Timed entry to upper terraces (foreigner ~US$25–35) since 2022; sunrise access ticketed separately. Local Buddhist community observes Waisak here in May — access restricted that day. Visitors dress modestly, walk clockwise around the stupas, do not touch reliefs.
questions: What are the rules for Borobudur?

entities.name: Prambanan
entities.description: Prambanan is a 9th-century Hindu temple complex — the largest in Indonesia — dedicated to the Trimurti (Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva). Belief tradition: Historical + revived Hindu practice (mostly Balinese Hindus visit for observances). Observance type: doctrinal (revived) + tourist-facing. UNESCO listed. Sarong + sash required for the main temples (rental included with ticket). Combine-ticket with Borobudur available. Dry-season Ramayana ballet in the outdoor amphitheatre most weekends — book ahead.
questions: What are the rules for Prambanan?

entities.name: Tirta Empul
entities.description: Pura Tirta Empul (in Tampaksiring, near Ubud) is the temple of holy spring water — a working Hindu pilgrimage site where Balinese come for melukat (purification bathing) at 30-plus spouts. Belief tradition: Balinese Hindu, active use. Observance type: doctrinal + contemporary practice. Visitors may bathe respectfully: change into a sarong + shorts in the changing area, do not use the two spouts reserved for funeral cleansing (marked; ask staff), do not photograph individuals mid-prayer, women should not enter the pools during menstruation.

entities.name: Uluwatu Temple
entities.description: Pura Luhur Uluwatu is one of the six sad kahyangan (major sea temples) protecting Bali. Belief tradition: Balinese Hindu. Observance type: doctrinal. Dramatic clifftop setting on Bali's south peninsula. Sarong + sash mandatory (included with entry, ~50k IDR foreigner). Macaque monkeys will snatch sunglasses, phones, hats — bag them before entering. The daily Kecak fire dance at sunset (starts ~18:00) is a cultural performance held in a nearby amphitheatre — not part of the temple ritual itself.
